summary:
An app that helps ships avoid Arctic sea ice. It detects ice using NASA NISAR radar images, predicts how the ice moves over multiple days, and checks whether a route stays clear of the ice when the ship passes.

An interactive route-planning tool. A model we trained detects sea ice and open water in NISAR images (HH, VV). Ice moves with a drift model, in 48 h steps:
next drift = a × previous drift + b × next wind + c × previous wind + d fitted by least squares on 30,769 examples of OSI SAF ice drift and wind. In the app, the Oct 2026 ice map drifts for 12 days. We focused on the Chukchi Sea, north of the Bering Strait.

As sea ice retreats, more ships with low ice class enter the Arctic. Ships can strike ice or be trapped by it; ice pressure can damage the hull and cause oil spills, and a trapped ship can run aground (NASA ARSET, 2023: https://www.earthdata.nasa.gov/learn/trainings/sar-detecting-monitoring-floods-sea-ice-subsidence-from-groundwater-extraction). Knowing where the ice will be lets operators plan safer routes.
details:
What it does and how it works
Ice Raider helps ships find a safe route through Arctic sea ice. It works in four steps. First, it finds the sea ice in radar images from NASA's new NISAR satellite, using a model we trained to tell ice from open water. Second, it measures how the ice moved between two satellite passes a day apart. Third, it predicts where the ice will drift over the next 12 days, mainly from the wind: sea ice moves at about 2% of the wind speed, turned slightly to the right of the wind, and our model learned this from eight years of satellite records of ice drift and wind. Fourth, an interactive map shows the ice moving day by day and checks a ship's route against the ice where it will be when the ship gets there, not where it was last seen.

Performance
Our ice detection was right about 90% of the time on satellite images it had never seen. To test the drift prediction fairly, we trained it on 2018–2023 and checked it on 2024–2026: over two days the ice typically drifts about 20 km, and our prediction was usually off by about 10 km, less than half the error of assuming the ice keeps its previous course (about 25 km). Compared with ice movement we measured ourselves in NISAR images, the one-day prediction was off by only 1.6 km after the ice had moved 10.7 km.

Benefits and intended impact
As Arctic ice retreats, more ships enter icy waters, many of them not strengthened for ice. Hitting ice or getting trapped by it can damage a ship, endanger its crew and cause oil spills (NASA ARSET, 2023). Ice Raider lets a planner see where the ice is heading, try a later departure day, or drag the route around the ice before setting sail. Areas no satellite has seen are marked "unknown", never "safe".

Try it yourself
Everything is in our public repository: https://github.com/SweetBoySavage/iceraider. The app runs on any laptop with Python and one command (python scripts/run_app.py); no radar data, accounts or special hardware are needed, because the ice maps are included.

Tools
Python for the data processing and models, and a simple web page (HTML, CSS, JavaScript) for the interactive map. Data: NASA NISAR radar images, European OSI SAF ice drift records, ERA5 wind data, a University of Bremen ice map to train the detection, and a global coastline from GSHHG (Global Self-consistent, Hierarchical, High-resolution Geography Database). The code was written with the help of an AI assistant (Claude), directed and checked by our team.

Innovations
Instead of only detecting ice using NISAR data, we also focused on tracking said ice. This is a dynamic approach, which we capture in a nice user friendly interface.

Limitations
NISAR also doesn't provide the radar channels for our area of interest around the Chukchi sea in early November, so our ice map is from October 2026. Also some regions are missing L-band data.

Hence we could also use the past wind data in our modelling. In the future when the latest NISAR would be available we could actually do prediction/forecasting in to the future!

Next steps
Check the predicted drift against GPS buoys that drift with the ice. Add ice thickness and how densely the ice is packed, since thick, tightly packed ice drifts less freely.
